newsitem.title: UK: Police on stand-by for rival N.Irish protests.
newsitem.headline: Police on stand-by for rival N.Irish protests.

text.p: A strong force of police was on alert in Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry on Saturday, to prevent trouble at demonstrations by pro-British Protestants and Irish Catholics.

Police sources said that the Apprentice Boys organisation would be allowed to march around the the city's ancient walls despite protests by Catholics who said they would hold a counter protest by Catholics.
The Apprentice Boys association march holds a special place in the history of pro-British Protestants.
In December 1688 thirteen apprentice boys closed the gates of the city of Derry against the approaching forces of deposed James II.

A subsequent siege was followed by the defeat of James at the Battle of the Boyne in July 1690 when the army of King William III, set on restoring Protestantism to the British Isles, defeated James's forces.
Police permission for the Protestant parade was given 30 minutes before the planned Apprentice Boys march.

Several hundered police were on duty and negotiations were going on between senior officers and Catholics protestors who said that they wanted 13 of their representatives to stage a protest along the contentious route.

The Apprentice Boys denied Catholic charges that their march plan was increasing instability in the British province, which has been on a tightrope since an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb attack two weeks ago stirred fears of retaliation by banned Protestant guerrillas.
The Apprentice Boys said that that they intended no insult to the Catholic residents by marching along a section of the walls overlooking the nationalist Bogside area.

In August British troops blocked off the walled section to defuse mounting sectarian tension over Apprentice Boys plans then to walk the route on the biggest day of their annual three-month "marching season", August 12.
The organisation called off their march and said they would walk the route "at a time of our own choosing".
Irish nationalist leader and Londonderry legislator John Hume appealed to Catholics on Friday to allow the Protestants to walk unhindered. He appealed to Catholics to call off their rival protest.
